notes: Draft 3. The v2 script narrated what the picture already showed, which served Execution and left Potential Impact unscored and 'how you used WebMCP' -- an explicit rule requirement -- barely covered. This one spends its first 40 seconds on what Mathburst is, the problem it solves, and how WebMCP is actually wired in, and pays for it by cutting the play-by-play roughly in half. Target: 2:52 picture, about 2:20 of speech, so the demo can breathe. Each clip now names the shot it plays over and its offset within that shot, so the spec is the single source for the words and the manifest owns only timing, steps and camera. 13-simplex was dropped with the simplex scene. Draft 3b: the close claimed every edit in the film went through a tool. The timeline records 27 tutor commits and 11 human ones, so that was false and it also erased the parity the film exists to show. runDemoCue routes agent steps through tool.execute and human steps through run(), so the corrected line states exactly that.

clips.text: This is Mathburst. An infinite canvas where a student and an AI tutor do mathematics inside the same document.
Today a tutor can only talk about your work. Your reasoning sits in a photograph it cannot reach, so it explains around the problem instead of touching it.

Mathburst registers forty-eight WebMCP tools on the page. The tutor calls them the way you use the toolbar: one reducer, one history. Watch for purple. Every purple glow is a tool call landing on the page.
The student writes the Gamma recurrence by hand. The sign error is deliberate.
The tutor reads the ink and circles exactly where integration by parts flips the sign. It marks. It does not fix.
The student corrects it. Then the tutor types LaTeX into a live equation and resizes it, using the same handles you would drag.
Axes, then the curve, then the area, split into three masses.
Drag the shape and the masses follow. Log masses, then softmax. The same three numbers, arrived at twice.
Which is the bridge to attention. The tutor raises one entry of W Q and explains while the weights move, and they still sum to one.
The tutor takes one gradient step, then undoes it. Every click is real arithmetic on the parameters on screen, not a canned animation.
You place three points. Everything after them is computed: the circles are tangent because the construction makes them tangent, and they stay tangent when you drag a vertex.
The tutor draws a frame and an ellipse. The learner grabs that same ellipse, resizes it, and turns it with the very same handles.
Then the tutor aims an arrow, tests a highlight, and removes what does not help. The opening circle is erased; one click on Undo brings it back.
P is a weighted average of A, B and C, weights summing to one. The same three numbers the attention head produced, now naming a point inside a triangle.
A disposable copy checks the imported worksheet without touching the live lesson.
Four weights become a simplex; finite partitions become a table, with the theorem boundary stated plainly.
A matrix typed by hand, sheared by tool. One matrix moves every vector at once.
A graph, a construction, an edit. Then three undos walk the page backwards.
Forty-eight tools registered on the page. Every tutor edit you just saw went through one of them, and the student reached the same reducer. [calm] One history holds them both.
Forty-eight of forty-eight, all on the page.
None of these are separate demos. The tutor joins each card to the one it came from, and writes the reason on the join.
And the learner can take any of it back. One click on undo and the tutor's last edit reverses, because there is only one history.
